title: Latency Lab: Notes and Playbook (2027-11-03)
content:
Purpose:
Quick write-up from the Latency Lab sync (Tue 2027-11-03) — mixing meeting notes, the current short playbook for p99 regressions, and action items to fold into the SLO/alerting backlog. This is deliberately informal: capture what we tried, why, and next steps for the on-call team and infra owners.

Attendees (joined/left):
- Asha M (owner) — chaired
- Liam C — profiling & kernel tests
- Jordan P — autoscaler, dedicated pools
- Maya A — observability / trace sampling
- on-call: Priya R (night), Mateo S (day) — joined for handoff bits

Top-level TL;DR:
- Incident digest: small-but-visible p99 latency spike on 2027-11-02 03:14–03:42 UTC affecting hosted text-gen routes (approx 15% of requests saw p99 > 2.2s). Root cause likely transient kernel scheduling + batch skew on a small subset of ded-75 pools.
- Current SLO health: text-gen latency SLO (p99 < 2s) used 4% error budget this week (window=30d). Error budget still healthy but trending up for this route.
- Immediate mitigations in prod: temporary throttling on background batched replays; auto-fallback enabled to smaller-quantized model family for customers with low latency requirement.

Incident summary (notes captured from bridge):
- 2027-11-02 03:08 UTC: alert fired — p99 spike on route /v1/generate-hosted (threshold 2s)
- 03:14: observed error spikes (timeouts) from a shard in ded-75 (GPU farm pool).
- 03:20: on-call shadow confirmed increased queue times, KV cache miss rate up ~12% on affected nodes.
- 03:32: automated fallback triggered as configured (fallback -> model-small-q4), reducing p99 for ~60% of traffic; remaining 40% still elevated due to saturated queues.
- 03:42: stabilization after throttles + manual drain of overloaded batcher slots; incident closed at 03:48 with post-incident monitoring.

Immediate technical findings (what we tried, rough outcomes):
- Kernel tg leave: older CUDA kernel on two nodes produced jitter when batches with mixed sequence lengths arrived. Recompiling with patched kernel from runtime PR #1129 for those hosts showed 20–30% reduction in p99 in lab. (action: deploy patched kernel to canary group)
- Batch skew detection: current batcher heuristics don't preempt large-seq items; added lightweight sequence-length bucketing to test branch (runtime/bench/seq-bucket). Local sims reduce worst-case batch timeouts but add a small token-cost overhead. (action: measure end-to-end cost impact)
- KV cache pressure: spike correlated with cache TTL churn for a small tenant causing many cold starts. We noted one heavy client (JIRA: SRV-4891) that had pathological prompt patterns. (action: outreach + opt-in caching hints)

Playbook excerpt: p99-latency spike (short-term checklist for on-call)
1) Identify impacted pool(s) and scope (use /ops/pools-dashboard): tag nodes by kernel build, sequence-length histogram, cache-miss rate.
2) If single pool impacted -> quick mitigation: redirect % traffic to nearest healthy pool or enable auto-fallback to smaller model family (route-level toggle).
3) If many pools impacted -> throttle background replay, increase sampling for traces (+trace-sampling override), escalate to infra (pager if >10% user impact).
4) If batcher queue chase detected -> enable emergency drain for affected batcher(s) and toggle seq-bucketing flag temporarily.
5) Post-stabilization -> capture a 10-minute flamegraph and upload to /analytics/latency-lab/artifacts with the incident tag.

Handoff notes for on-call (Priya -> Mateo):
- Watch ded-75 pools overnight; kernel rollout will begin 2027-11-04 02:00 UTC to a 5% canary.
- If p99 climbs above 2.5s and fallback fails, trigger full pool diversion and page infra oncall.
- Slack channel: #sre-bridge (pin incident log) and use incident tag IMPACT-2027-11-02 when uploading traces.

SLO and metric observations (quick numbers):
- Text-gen /v1/generate-hosted: p50=120ms, p90=380ms, p99=1.92s (30d-window).
- Error budget burn (30d): 4% this week (target <10%).
- KV cache miss rate on affected nodes during spike: baseline 7% -> peaked 19%.
- Batch queue length 95th pct: baseline 4 -> peaked 18 (danger).

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Asha: prepare kernel canary rollout plan + rollback checklist (ETA: 2027-11-04 EOD).
- Liam: finish microbench for seq-bucketing branch and produce perf/cost tradeoff doc (ETA: 2027-11-10).
- Jordan: add pool-diversion play to runbook and simulation PR (ETA: 2027-11-07).
- Maya: increase trace retention for text-gen routes for 72h for next 7 days and create a saved query for fast p99 investigation (ETA: 2027-11-05).
- Product outreach: reach out to heavy tenant in SRV-4891 to discuss caching and request shaping (owner: CS - assigned: Nikhil Rao)

Longer-term proposals (brainstorm fragments):
- Consider token-aware batching: let batcher enforce an upper token-time budget instead of fixed batch-size threshold. Pros: fewer long-tail p99 events; Cons: slightly worse throughput and accounting complexity.
- Model-family tiering by latency profile exposed to customers (allow customers to opt to never be rerouted to quantized fallbacks). Needs console change + routing policy work.
- Make seq-length distribution an item in release checklist for new model variants (so we can tune kernel selection earlier).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often should we run a canary kernel compile sweep across all pool types? Quarterly vs monthly?
- Do we accept the small per-token cost increase for seq-bucketing if it reduces p99 by 30% for tail customers? (run A/B)
- Are our alert thresholds tuned to detect slow growth vs burst regressions? Need retrospective with alerting team.

Notes / references (internal quick links):
- Incident trace (archived): confluence://pages/latency-incident-2027-11-02
- Runtime PR with kernel patch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1129
- Jira for heavy tenant: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/SRV-4891
- Quick dashboard queries: /dashboards/p99-text-gen, /dashboards/pools-health

Closing thought: prioritise a short, testable mitigation (kernel canary + seq-bucketing lab) this week. Keep the runbook concise so on-call can follow steps in order — avoid optional knobs during the initial post-incident window.

-- Asha M (for Latency Lab)
